clinicalPearls: The mildest of the inherited insulin-receptor disorders, typically from heterozygous INSR mutations and often presenting in adolescent or young adult women
Classic triad of severe insulin resistance, acanthosis nigricans, and hyperandrogenism (hirsutism, oligomenorrhoea, polycystic ovaries) in a lean, non-obese individual
Distinguished from ordinary polycystic ovary syndrome by the disproportionate degree of insulin resistance relative to body weight
Marked hyperinsulinaemia is present, and glucose tolerance may be normal early before overt diabetes develops
Ovarian theca-cell stimulation by high insulin drives the hyperandrogenism (an overlap with the acquired HAIR-AN picture)

Because the defect is at the insulin receptor, management uses insulin sensitisers and, in more severe cases, recombinant IGF-1 for severe insulin resistance; leptin has a limited role when leptin is not deficient
It sits at the mild end of the INSR spectrum, far less severe than Rabson-Mendenhall or Donohue syndromes
Diagnosis rests on the lean hyperandrogenic phenotype with disproportionate hyperinsulinaemia and INSR genetics
reference.pathophysiology: Type A insulin resistance syndrome is a genetic insulin-signalling defect, usually from heterozygous mutations in the insulin receptor gene (INSR), that impairs insulin action without the obesity, autoimmunity, or lipodystrophy that cause other insulin-resistant states. Reduced receptor function forces compensatory hyperinsulinaemia; the excess insulin acts on ovarian theca cells to stimulate androgen production, generating hirsutism, menstrual disturbance, and polycystic ovaries, while impaired insulin action on skin promotes acanthosis nigricans. Because affected individuals are typically lean, the severity of insulin resistance is out of proportion to body weight, and overt insulin-resistant diabetes may emerge over time as compensation fails.
additionalDifferentials: Polycystic ovary syndrome with ordinary insulin resistance
Type B insulin resistance from anti-insulin-receptor antibodies
additionalInvestigations: Fasting insulin and C-peptide demonstrating marked hyperinsulinaemia
Androgen profile (testosterone and related androgens) for hyperandrogenism
Pelvic ultrasound for polycystic ovarian morphology
INSR gene sequencing, with autoantibody testing to exclude type B resistance
Lipid profile and leptin to characterise the metabolic state
redFlags: Progression to overt, difficult-to-control insulin-resistant diabetes
Rapidly worsening virilisation suggesting an alternative androgen source
Features suggesting type B (autoimmune) insulin resistance
Severe metabolic derangement disproportionate to body habitus
reference.prognosis: The prognosis is more favourable than the severe childhood INSR disorders; many patients are managed for years with insulin sensitisers, though progression to overt diabetes and the burden of hyperandrogenism require ongoing care.
pitfalls: Labelling the presentation as ordinary polycystic ovary syndrome and missing the disproportionate insulin resistance
Overlooking a lean body habitus as a clue against obesity-driven resistance
Failing to separate genetic type A from autoimmune type B insulin resistance
Assuming leptin replacement will help when leptin is not deficient
Not confirming the diagnosis with INSR genetic testing
references: Endocrine Society clinical practice guidance on severe insulin resistance
management: Insulin sensitisers, principally metformin and where appropriate a thiazolidinedione, to counter the receptor-level insulin resistance and compensatory hyperinsulinaemia
Recombinant IGF-1 (mecasermin) as targeted therapy in more severe insulin resistance, bypassing the defective insulin receptor via the IGF-1 receptor
Management of hyperandrogenism with a combined oral contraceptive and an anti-androgen such as spironolactone for hirsutism and menstrual disturbance
Surveillance for progression to overt insulin-resistant diabetes with periodic glucose and HbA1c monitoring as beta-cell compensation fails
Fertility and reproductive care addressing oligomenorrhoea and polycystic ovarian dysfunction
Multidisciplinary input from endocrinology and clinical genetics, with dietetic support even in lean patients
Genetic counselling and family assessment given the heritable INSR mutation
